desc:
A lumberjack must collect at least need metres of wood. He sets his saw to an integer height H and cuts every tree in the row trees (given as heights in metres) that is taller than H: the part above H falls and is collected, the part below stays. A tree not taller than H gives nothing.

To spare the forest, he wants the saw as high as possible. Return the largest integer H ≥ 0 for which the collected wood is at least need. The total height of all trees is guaranteed to be at least need, so H = 0 always works.

Example: trees = [20, 15, 10, 17], need = 7. At H = 15 he collects 5 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 7, at H = 16 only 4 + 1 = 5, so the answer is 15.
hints: Compute the wood collected for a single chosen height first. How does it change if you raise the saw?
Raising the saw never increases the collected wood. So the heights that work form a prefix 0..H*, and you want its last element.
Binary search H in [0, max(trees)]. Use the upper-mid (lo + hi + 1) // 2 when you move lo = mid on success, otherwise the loop never ends.
editorial: Define wood(H) = sum(max(0, t - H)). It is non-increasing in H, equals the full total at H = 0 and is 0 at H = max(trees). Therefore the predicate wood(H) ≥ need is true on a prefix of the heights and false afterwards; we look for the last true position.

When searching for the last true value, round the midpoint up so that lo = mid always makes progress. Each evaluation is a linear scan, so the total is O(n log max(trees)) time and O(1) space. Sorting plus prefix sums can answer each probe faster, but the linear scan is already fast enough here.
